faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks. For a standard full-time role, assume 38 hours per week. For example, $30 per hour × 38 hours × 52 weeks = $59,280 per year. This gives a gross annual figure before tax and super.

faqs.q: What is casual loading and how does it affect my pay?
faqs.a: Casual loading is an extra 25% paid on top of the base hourly rate to compensate for not receiving paid leave. The Fair Work Commission sets the casual loading at 25% of the national minimum wage. For award-free casual employees, the minimum casual rate is $33.05 per hour (from 1 July 2026). When using our timesheet, tick the casual loading checkbox to add 25% to your base rate.

faqs.q: How is superannuation calculated on my pay?
faqs.a: Superannuation is paid on top of your gross earnings at the super guarantee rate of 12% (from 1 July 2026). It applies to ordinary time earnings up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, on a $60,000 annual salary, your employer must contribute an extra $7,200 into your super fund. Super is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional cost for the employer.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting Hourly Rates to Annual Pay: The 38-Hour Week, Fortnight, and 52-Week Year

Whether you're comparing your earnings to a headline figure like the **Haaland salary** or simply working out your own budget, understanding how to convert an hourly rate to an annual salary is essential. In Australia, the standard full-time working week is 38 hours, and the year is 52 weeks. This gives a straightforward formula: **hourly rate × hours per week × 52 = annual gross pay**.

For example, if you earn $30 per hour and work 38 hours each week, your annual salary is $30 × 38 × 52 = $59,280. This is your gross income before tax, Medicare levy, and superannuation. The same calculation works for any hourly rate, from the national minimum wage to a six-figure executive package.

### The National Minimum Wage and Award Rates

From 1 July 2026, the national minimum wage is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week, as set by the Fair Work Commission. This is the minimum for adult employees not covered by an award or agreement. Many industries have higher award rates that apply depending on your classification and role. Use the Fair Work Ombudsman's Pay Calculator to check your specific minimum.

### Casual Loading: Adding 25%

If you are a casual employee, you are entitled to a 25% casual loading on top of the base hourly rate. This compensates for not receiving paid leave such as annual leave and sick leave. For award-free casuals, the minimum casual rate is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 × 1.25). When using [the timesheet](/), tick the casual loading checkbox to automatically add 25% to your entered base rate. Do not enter a rate that already includes casual loading; the tool handles it for you.

### From Weekly to Fortnightly Pay

Many employers pay fortnightly. To find your fortnightly gross pay, simply multiply your weekly pay by two. For the national minimum wage, weekly pay is $1,004.90, so fortnightly pay is $2,009.80. This is useful for budgeting and comparing salary offers.

### Tax and Medicare Levy

Your annual gross pay is not what you take home. The Australian Taxation Office applies progressive tax rates for 2026–27:
- Nil on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Additionally, most residents pay a Medicare levy of 2% of taxable income. The tax-free threshold and Medicare levy reduction thresholds apply. Our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) page provides a detailed breakdown.

### Superannuation Paid on Top

Superannuation is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional contribution your employer must make. From 1 July 2026, the super guarantee rate is 12% of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. For example, on a $60,000 salary, your employer adds $7,200 to your super fund. This is separate from your gross pay and is paid on top. See [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) for more.

### Putting It All Together: The Haaland Salary Example

Even a globally famous figure like the reported **Haaland salary** can be converted to an hourly rate using this method. If a footballer earns, say, $20 million per year, dividing by 52 weeks gives $384,615 per week, and dividing by 38 hours gives an hourly rate of over $10,000. While most of us won't earn that, the same formula applies to any salary. Understanding the conversion helps you compare job offers, negotiate pay, and plan your finances.

### Important Assumptions

This conversion assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, penalty rates, or allowances. It also assumes no salary sacrifice arrangements. For award-covered employees, your actual pay may include additional loadings or penalties. Always check your award or agreement using the [pay guides](/blog) or the Fair Work Ombudsman's resources.

### Using Our Timesheet

To quickly convert your hourly rate to annual, fortnightly, or weekly figures, use [the timesheet](/). Enter your base hourly rate, select casual loading if applicable, and the tool calculates gross annual pay, tax, Medicare, and super. It uses the official 2026–27 tax rates and 12% super guarantee. Remember, super is paid on top of your gross pay, not deducted from it.

### Summary

- **Formula:** hourly rate × 38 hours × 52 weeks = annual gross pay
- **National minimum wage:** $26.44/hr, $1,004.90/week, $52,254.80/year
- **Casual loading:** add 25% to base rate (e.g., $33.05/hr)
- **Fortnightly pay:** weekly pay × 2
- **Tax:** progressive rates plus 2% Medicare levy
- **Super:** 12% on top, up to $270,830 contribution base

Whether you're comparing your own earnings to the **Haaland salary** or just checking your next pay rise, this simple conversion gives you a clear picture of your annual income.
